Could clean cooking be one of the most powerful opportunities to advance health, gender equality and sustainable development?
 
On the International Day of Clean Air for blue skies, I keep coming back to clean cooking.
 
Nearly 2 billion people still lack access to clean cooking. In rural Sub-Saharan Africa, only 7% of the population has access to clean cooking fuels.
 
The consequences reach far beyond the kitchen. Household air pollution caused an estimated 2.9 million deaths in 2021, while polluting cooking also affects productivity, gender equality and economic opportunity.
 
Yet the investment gap remains striking.
 
Around US$2.5 billion is invested in clean cooking solutions each year, less than a third of the US$8 billion needed annually to achieve universal access. Meanwhile, the health, environmental and productivity costs associated with polluting cooking are estimated at US$2.4–4 trillion every year.
 
For me, this makes clean cooking not simply an energy technology, but a development priority across the Global South.
 
Three shifts can help accelerate progress:
🔌 Integrate clean cooking into national energy planning. Nepal aims for 25% of households to adopt electric cooking by 2030, linking clean cooking directly to wider electrification efforts.
💰 Make finance reach the households most often left behind. Grants, subsidies and blended finance can help reduce upfront costs for rural and low-income communities.
🗺️ Use data and digital tools to target solutions better. Mapping grid reliability, consumer demand and e-cooking potential can help direct investment where it can deliver the greatest impact.
 
Clean air, energy access and development should not be treated as separate agendas.
 
Clean cooking can improve health, expand opportunity and make a just energy transition more inclusive at the same time.
